Explanation: The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), or VB-G
RAM G, is a landmark legislation passed in late 2025 that replaces the long-standing MGNREGA
(Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) of 2005. Operating under the
Ministry of Rural Development, this new mission is designed to modernize rural employment and
align it with the national vision of a developed India by 2047. The mission functions by enhancing
the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days of unskilled manual work per
rural household in a financial year. To ensure that public works do not compete with farming, the
law allows state governments to implement an agricultural pause of up to 60 days during peak
sowing and harvesting seasons, ensuring labor availability for farmers while still providing 125
days of work during the remaining 305 days of the year.
The administrative and planning framework of VB-G RAM G is deeply decentralized and
technology-driven. Every Gram Panchayat is mandated to create a Viksit Gram Panchayat Plan,
which identifies local needs and is integrated into the national spatial system via PM Gati Shakti.
All physical assets created through this labor—ranging from water security structures and core
rural infrastructure to livelihood assets and climate resilience works—are tracked through the
Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack. The scheme follows a centrally sponsored
model with a revised 60:40 fund-sharing pattern between the Centre and States (90:10 for North-
Eastern and Himalayan states). To maintain accountability, the mission uses biometric
authentication for attendance, Al-based fraud detection, and real-time digital monitoring,
ensuring that wages are paid weekly and that states are liable for unemployment allowances if
they fail to provide work within 15 days of a demand.

Explanation: The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) is the apex statutory body in
India responsible for the over-arching management of Project Tiger and the country’s tiger
reserves. It was established to provide legal teeth to tiger conservation efforts, ensuring that the
central and state governments work in a coordinated, accountable framework.
Key Facts and Establishment
Date of Establishment: The NTCA was officially formed in December 2005.
+ Legal Status: It is a statutory body under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change (MoEF&CC). It was constituted under the enabling provisions of the Wildlife
(Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2006.
+ Leadership: The Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change serves as the
Chairperson, while the State Minister of Environment serves as the Vice-Chairperson.
Primary Objectives
The NTCA was created with several specific goals to streamline tiger conservation:
+ Statutory Authority: To provide legal backing to Project Tiger so that its directives are
mandatory and legally binding.
+ Accountability: To foster a memorandum of understanding (MoU) based relationship between
the Centre and States, ensuring clear responsibilities for tiger reserve management.
Parliamentary Oversight: To provide regular reports and updates to the Parliament of India
regarding the status of tigers and their habitats.
* Community Welfare: To address the livelihood and developmental interests of local people
living in the buffer and fringe areas of tiger reserves.
Associated Projects and Technological Initiatives
The NTCA spearheads several high-tech and high-impact projects:
Project Tiger: The flagship centrally sponsored scheme that provides financial and technical
support to tiger-range states.
M-STrIPES: The "Monitoring System for Tigers - Intensive Protection and Ecological Status"
is a software-based tool used by forest guards for digital patrolling and real-time data
collection.

All India Tiger Estimation (AITE): A massive scientific exercise conducted every four years to
estimate the tiger population. The 2018-19 cycle was recognized by the Guinness World
Records as the world's largest camera-trap wildlife survey.
* Project Cheetah: The NTCA is the nodal agency for the reintroduction of cheetahs in India,
including the ongoing expansion at Kuno National Park and Gandhi Sagar Sanctuary as of
2026.
Major Activities and Functions
Tiger Conservation Plans (TCP): The NTCA evaluates and approves the conservation plans
submitted by state governments for each reserve.
* Management Effectiveness Evaluation (MEE): It conducts periodic independent assessments of
tiger reserves to grade their performance and identify gaps.
+ Special Tiger Protection Force (STPF): It provides funding and guidelines for the creation of
specialized, armed units to combat poaching in sensitive landscapes.
Human-Wildlife Conflict Mitigation: It issues Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for
handling tiger dispersals, straying incidents, and active management of tiger populations.
* Corridor Management: Identifying and securing tiger corridors to ensure genetic flow between
isolated populations.

Explanation: The Gajraj system, also known as the Gajraj Suraksha, is an indigenous artificial
intelligence-based Intrusion Detection System (IDS) developed by Indian Railways to eliminate
elephant-train collisions. Operating under the Ministry of Railways, the system utilizes
Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) technology through existing underground optical fiber cables
(OFC) laid alongside railway tracks. These cables act as sensitive vibration sensors that detect the
specific pressure waves and seismic signatures generated by the footsteps of approaching
elephants. The AI model then analyzes these signals in real-time, capable of distinguishing
elephant movement from other disturbances with a reported accuracy of 99.5%.
When an elephant is detected within a 200-meter radius of the tracks, the system immediately
triggers automated alerts to various stakeholders, including loco pilots, station masters, and
divisional control rooms. This early warning allows train drivers to proactively reduce speed or
stop the train before entering the vulnerable zone. Initially pioneered by the Northeast Frontier
Railway (NFR) in December 2022, the system has successfully scaled up to cover critical corridors
across states like Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. As of early 2026, the
project has expanded significantly across the national rail network, proving to be a vital tool in
balancing infrastructure operations with wildlife conservation.

Agreements with Key Partner Countries
Namibia (July 2022): This was the first country to sign a Memorandum of Understanding
(MoU) with India. The agreement focused on wildlife conservation and sustainable biodiversity
management. It facilitated the first batch of eight cheetahs (five females and three males) that
arrived in India on September 17, 2022. The MoU also covers the exchange of expertise,
training of professionals in wildlife management, and sharing of technical know-how in
monitoring techniques.
South Africa (January 2023): India signed a comprehensive MoU with South Africa that
outlines a long-term collaboration. The agreement initially provided for the translocation of 12
cheetahs, which arrived in February 20238. Critically, the pact includes a provision to
translocate an additional 12 cheetahs annually for the next eight to ten years to ensure genetic
diversity. The MoU is reviewed every five years and includes bilateral custodianship
arrangements and joint research on large carnivore management.
Botswana (November 2025): During a state visit by President Droupadi Murmu, India and
Botswana formalized a new pact for the translocation of eight cheetahs. These animals,
sourced from the Kalahari region, are scheduled to arrive in India by February 2026. This
agreement marks an expansion of the project’s source countries to further strengthen the
meta-population and diversify the gene pool of the cats in Indian habitats.
Objectives of the International Collaborations The overarching goal of these diplomatic and
scientific agreements is to re-establish the functional role of the cheetah in India's grassland
and semi-arid ecosystems. The collaborative framework includes:
Capacity Building: Exchange of forest officers and scientists between India and African
nations for hands-on training.
* Scientific Research: Sharing data on predator-prey dynamics and health management.
* Global Conservation: Contributing to the global survival of the species by expanding its range
outside of the African continent.

Explanation: Project Cheetah is a historic global conservation initiative aimed at reintroducing
the cheetah to India after it was officially declared extinct in the country in 1952. Launched on
September 17, 2022, it is spearheaded by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)
under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The project represents the first
intercontinental wild-to-wild translocation of a large carnivore, utilizing Kuno National Park in
Madhya Pradesh as its primary site due to its suitable grassland-savanna habitat and low human
density.
As of early January 2026, the project has reached several critical biological milestones. The total
cheetah population in India currently stands at 30 to 32 individuals. A major breakthrough
occurred in November 2025 when Mukhi, the first female cheetah born on Indian soil in March
2023, gave birth to a litter of five cubs. This event marked the first second-generation breeding
success of the program, demonstrating that India-born cheetahs can successfully adapt and
reproduce in their new environment. Of the current population, approximately 19 to 21 individuals
are India-born cubs and sub-adults, while the remainder are founder animals from the original
Namibian and South African batches.

The project is now entering a consolidation and expansion phase. While Kuno National Park
remains the focal point, the landscape is being expanded to include the Gandhi Sagar Wildlife
Sanctuary and eventually the Noradehi Wildlife Sanctuary to establish a larger, connected

formalized with Botswana for the translocation of eight additional cheetahs, including adult
females and cubs, who are expected to arrive in India by February 2026. This long-term strategy
aims to establish a self-sustaining population of 60 to 70 cheetahs across 17,000 square kilometers
of restored grassland ecosystems by 2032.

Explanation: In India, the National Air Quality Index (AQI) is calculated based on the ambient
concentration of eight specific pollutants. These pollutants were selected because they have short-
term National Ambient Air Quality Standards prescribed for them, allowing the government to
monitor and communicate health risks effectively to the public.
The eight elements included in the calculation are:
* Particulate Matter (PM10)
Particulate Matter (PM2.5)
Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2)
Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)
* Carbon Monoxide (CO)
* Ground-level Ozone (O03)
+ Ammonia (NH3)
* Lead (Pb)
To determine the overall AQI for a specific location, sub-indices are calculated for each of these
pollutants. According to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) guidelines, an AQI can only
be calculated if data for at least three pollutants are available, and one of those three must
necessarily be either PM10 or PM2.5. The final AQI reported is the highest sub-index among the
pollutants measured, following the "worst-case" principle to ensure public health is prioritized.

Explanation: The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) is a set of emergency measures
implemented to combat air pollution in the Delhi-National Capital Region (NCR). It is a statutory
framework managed by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) in collaboration
with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Rather than being a year-round
policy, GRAP is a reactive and predictive mechanism that triggers specific restrictions based on
the severity of air quality, categorized by the Air Quality Index (AQJ). As of late 2025 and early
2026, the plan has been updated to be more stringent and preemptive, allowing authorities to
invoke higher stages based on meteorological forecasts from the IMD and IITM even before the
AQI actually reaches critical levels.

The plan operates through four distinct stages, with each higher stage including all measures from
the previous ones:
+ Stage 1 (Poor Air Quality, AQI 201-300): This stage focuses on basic dust control at
construction sites, mechanical road sweeping, and a strict ban on open garbage burning. It also
involves intensifying the enforcement of pollution norms for vehicles and advising the public to
minimize activities that cause dust.
Stage 2 (Very Poor Air Quality, AQI 301-400): Measures are intensified to include daily water
sprinkling on roads to suppress dust. Restrictions are placed on the use of diesel generator sets
except for emergency services. This stage also encourages the use of public transport by
increasing the frequency of metro and bus services and introduces higher parking fees to
discourage private vehicle use.
+ Stage 3 (Severe Air Quality, AQI 401-450): This stage involves a blanket ban on non-essential
construction and demolition activities. It also imposes strict restrictions on the plying of older
vehicles, specifically banning BS-3 petrol and BS-4 diesel four-wheelers in Delhi and
surrounding NCR districts. State governments may also choose to close schools for younger
children.
+ Stage 4 (Severe Plus Air Quality, AQI >450): This is the emergency stage. It prohibits the
entry of all non-essential trucks into Delhi, except those carrying essential commodities or
providing essential services. Only electric, CNG, or BS-6 diesel trucks are typically permitted.
Governments may mandate 50 percent work-from-home for offices and shift all school classes
to an online mode.
In early January 2026, CAQM revoked Stage 3 measures in Delhi-NCR after the air quality
improved to the poor category, though Stages 1 and 2 remain in force as preventive measures.

Explanation: Particulate matter (PM) is categorized by size, and both PM 10 and PM 2.5 pose
significant health risks because they are small enough to be inhaled deep into the respiratory
system. The primary difference in their health impact stems from how far they can travel into the
body.
Health Effects of PM 10 PM 10 refers to inhalable particles with diameters of 10 micrometers or
less (about one-seventh the width of a human hair).
Respiratory Irritation: These particles are generally deposited in the upper respiratory tract,
including the nose, mouth, and throat. They often cause immediate irritation, leading to
coughing, wheezing, and sore throats.
+ Worsening of Lung Diseases: Exposure can significantly aggravate existing conditions like
asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), leading to more frequent attacks
and increased hospital visits.
Eye and Sinus Issues: Because they are larger, they are more likely to cause physical irritation
to the eyes and nasal passages.
Health Effects of PM 2.5 PM 2.5 refers to fine particles with diameters of 2.5 micrometers or
less. These are considered much more dangerous because their tiny size allows them to bypass
the body’s natural defenses.

Deep Lung Penetration: PM 2.5 can travel past the upper airways and settle deep within the
lung alveoli (air sacs), where they can cause tissue inflammation and long-term scarring.
* Bloodstream Entry: These particles are so small that they can cross the lung-blood barrier and
enter the circulatory system. Once in the blood, they can travel to other organs, including the
heart and brain.
* Cardiovascular Impact: Exposure is strongly linked to serious heart-related issues, including
non-fatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeats (arrhythmia), and strokes.
Systemic Health Risks: Long-term exposure is associated with premature death in people with
heart or lung disease, reduced lung development in children, and an increased risk of
developing diabetes and certain types of cancer.

Explanation: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
The Environment (Protection) Act (EPA), 1986, serves as an umbrella legislation that provides the
Central Government with broad powers to coordinate the activities of various authorities
established under earlier laws like the Water and Air Acts. It was enacted under Article 253 of the
Constitution following the Bhopal Gas Tragedy to implement decisions made at the 1972
Stockholm Conference. In recent years, specifically through the Environment (Protection)
Amendment Rules, 2023, and subsequent 2024 notifications, the government has focused on
"decriminalizing" environmental regulations by replacing criminal imprisonment for minor
technical violations with significant monetary penalties. This shift aims to improve the ease of
doing business while maintaining high penalties for serious ecological damage. While its formal
short title remains the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, it is now often referenced in regulatory
policy as the primary framework for the Green Credit Program and the LiFE (Lifestyle for
Environment) initiative.
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Originally enacted in 1974 to prevent and control water pollution and maintain the
"wholesomeness" of water, this act led to the establishment of the Central and State Pollution
Control Boards. The law underwent a major transformation with the Water (Prevention and
Control of Pollution) Amendment Act, 2024. This amendment introduced a fundamental shift by
decriminalizing several minor, procedural, or first-time offenses that previously carried jail terms
of up to six years, replacing them with a penalty-based system ranging from 10,000 to 15 lakh
rupees. Furthermore, the 2024 Act empowers the Central Government to exempt certain low-
polluting industrial categories from obtaining the mandatory "Consent to Establish" or "Consent
to Operate" from State Boards, streamlining the regulatory process for green and orange category
industries.
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972
The Wild Life (Protection) Act provides the legal framework for the protection of various species of
wild animals, birds, and plants, and for the management of their habitats. A landmark change
occurred through the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (which came into force in 2023),
which officially changed the long title of the act to include the "conservation and management" of
wildlife rather than just "protection." A major highlight of this amendment was the rationalization
of its schedules; the previous six schedules were reduced to four. Schedule I now provides the

highest level of protection, Schedule II covers species with a lesser degree of protection, Schedule
III is dedicated to protected plants, and the newly created Schedule IV is dedicated to specimens
listed under the CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna
and Flora). The act also now includes specific provisions for the regulation of invasive alien species
and the management of conservation reserves.
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
The Forest (Conservation) Act was originally designed to restrict the use of forest land for non-
forest purposes without central approval. In 2023, the act was significantly amended and renamed
as the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, which translates to the Forest
(Conservation and Augmentation) Act. This new name reflects a shift in focus toward not just
protecting existing forests but also augmenting forest cover and carbon stocks to meet India's "Net
Zero" targets. The 2023 amendment specifies that the act only applies to land notified as forest
under the Indian Forest Act, 1927, or recorded in government records on or after October 25, 1980.
Crucially, it exempts strategic linear projects of national importance (such as roads or railways)
within 100 km of India’s international borders from the requirement of forest clearance, which has
been a point of significant environmental and strategic debate.

Explanation: The Supreme Court of India has established the right to clean air as a fundamental
right through several landmark judgments, evolving the interpretation of Article 21 (Right to Life)
over several decades.
Foundational Judgments
While the Constitution does not explicitly mention the environment in the Fundamental Rights
section, the judiciary bridged this gap by linking it to the right to live with dignity.
+ Subhash Kumar vs. State of Bihar (1991): This is the definitive case where the Supreme Court
explicitly stated that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to the enjoyment of
pollution-free water and air for the full enjoyment of life. The court ruled that if anything
endangers or impairs that quality of life in derogation of laws, a citizen has the right to move
the Supreme Court under Article 32.
+ M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case, 1996): In this case concerning the
protection of the Taj Mahal from industrial pollution, the Court reaffirmed that the right to
clean air is a part of the right to life. It invoked the Precautionary Principle and the Polluter
Pays Principle to order the closure or relocation of coal-consuming industries in the area.
Recent Landmark Expansion (2024)
In a major legal development in early 2024, the Supreme Court further expanded this
jurisprudence to include climate change.
+ M.K. Ranjitsinh vs. Union of India (2024): A bench led by the Chief Justice of India ruled that
people have a right against the adverse effects of climate change. The court observed that the
right to a clean environment and the right against climate change are two sides of the same
coin. It noted that as the havoc caused by climate change (including worsening air pollution
and rising temperatures) increases, it is necessary to articulate this as a distinct fundamental
right under Article 21 and Article 14 (Right to Equality).
The Court uses two key Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Duties to
support these Article 21 rulings:

Explanation: The Narmada River, often called the lifeline of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, flows
through three Indian states during its 1,312 km journey from the Amarkantak Plateau to the
Arabian Sea.
States the Narmada Flows Through
* Madhya Pradesh: This is the state where the river originates and spends the majority of its
course, covering approximately 1,077 km. It flows through prominent cities like Jabalpur,
Narmadapuram (Hoshangabad), and Maheshwar.
Maharashtra: The river serves as a natural boundary between Madhya Pradesh and
Maharashtra for a short stretch of about 35 km and then between Maharashtra and Gujarat
for another 39 km. The actual length flowing strictly within Maharashtra territory is relatively
small, but the state is a key stakeholder in the river's water management.
+ Gujarat: The final stretch of the river, approximately 161 km, lies in Gujarat. It flows through
the fertile plains of Bharuch and eventually empties into the Gulf of Knambhat.
Narmada Basin Coverage
While the river physically flows through the three states mentioned above, its drainage basin (the
area from which it collects water) is slightly broader, covering parts of four states:

The prevalence of tank irrigation in Southern India is primarily driven by the unique geological
and topographical characteristics of the Peninsular plateau, which make other forms of irrigation
like canals or wells highly difficult to implement.
Geological and Topographical Factors
+ Hard Rock Structure: The Deccan Plateau is composed of ancient, hard crystalline rocks that
are non-porous and impervious. This makes it extremely difficult and expensive to dig deep
wells or borewells compared to the soft alluvial soils of Northern India.
Impervious Surface: Because the underlying rock does not allow water to seep through easily,
there is very little natural percolation. This prevents the formation of large underground
aquifers but makes the surface ideal for catching and storing rainwater in natural or artificial
depressions.
Undulating Terrain: The landscape of South India is naturally uneven with many natural
depressions and valleys. This topography allows for the easy construction of small earthen
dams or bunds across streams to impound water, creating "tanks" with minimal engineering
effort.
Hydrological and Climatic Reasons
+ Seasonal Rivers: Unlike the perennial Himalayan rivers of the North, the rivers in Southern
India (like the Krishna, Kaveri, and Godavari) are rain-fed and seasonal. They often dry up
during the summer, making year-round canal irrigation unreliable. Tanks act as vital storage
reservoirs that hold monsoon water for use during the dry months.
+ Torrential Rainfall: The region often receives intense bursts of rainfall during the monsoon.
Without tanks, this water would quickly run off into the sea due to the hard, rocky surface.
Tanks capture this "torrential" runoff, preserving it for agricultural use.
Economic and Social Factors
+ Low Construction Cost: Since many tanks utilize natural depressions in the rocky terrain, the
cost of building them is relatively low. Small-scale tanks can even be maintained by individual
farmers or local village communities.
+ Ancillary Benefits: Beyond irrigation, these tanks serve multiple purposes, including providing
drinking water for cattle, supporting local fisheries, and helping to slightly recharge the
immediate local water table.
+ Scattered Agricultural Fields: The nature of farming in the plateau region involves scattered
patches of cultivable land. Large-scale canal networks are often not viable for such fragmented
fields, making localized tanks a more practical solution.

The Three Lists of the Seventh Schedule
The Constitution classifies all legislative subjects into three functional categories:
+ List I - Union List: This list contains subjects of national importance that require a uniform
law across the entire country. The Union Parliament has exclusive power to legislate on these
matters. It originally contained 97 subjects but currently includes 100.

and Citizenship.

legislation is beneficial to cater to specific state needs. State Legislatures have exclusive power
to make laws here under normal circumstances. It originally had 66 subjects but now has 61.
o Examples: Police, Public Order, Agriculture, Public Health, Sanitation, Local Government, and
Fisheries.
List III — Concurrent List: This list covers subjects where uniformity is desirable but not
essential, allowing both the Union Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws. The
concept was borrowed from the Australian Constitution. It originally had 47 subjects and now
has 52.

Protection of Wild Animals.

The Lokpal is a statutory anti-corruption body established as the national ombudsman of India

minorities, or women.

high-level selection committee and a search committee. The selection committee is chaired by the

Lok Sabha, the Chief Justice of India (or a nominated judge), and an eminent jurist. This
committee relies on a panel of names recommended by a search committee composed of at least
eight eminent persons. Once appointed, the chairperson and members hold office for a term of five
years or until they reach the age of 70. This rigorous selection process is intended to ensure that
the ombudsman remains autonomous and insulated from political interference while exercising its
significant powers of investigation and prosecution.
